group.passage: Most of us try hard never to feel bored, and with a phone in every pocket, escaping the feeling has never been easier. But is boredom really something to run away from? In the texts below, a science writer explains what researchers have learned about it, and a high school student describes what happened when she gave it a chance.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: What Boredom Is For
passage_parts.text: Boredom is often described as simply having nothing to do, but psychologists define it more precisely: it is the unpleasant feeling of wanting to be engaged in a satisfying activity and being unable to find one. Seen this way, boredom is not a sign of laziness. It works more like an alarm, telling us that what we are doing no longer meets our needs and that it is time to move on to something else. Boredom may also have a hidden benefit. When the mind has nothing to hold onto, it tends to wander, and during these moments of daydreaming people often make surprising connections between ideas. In one well-known experiment, people who first spent some time on a very dull task came up with more creative ideas afterward than people who had skipped it. The problem today is that we seldom let boredom last long enough to do us any good. The moment we feel restless, we reach for a screen, and researchers suspect that this quick fix may actually leave us feeling more bored in the long run.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: My Week Without a Phone
passage_parts.text: Last month, our English teacher asked the whole class to spend one week without phones after school. For the first two days, I was climbing the walls. Whenever I sat on the bus, my hand kept reaching for a pocket that was empty, and I spent the whole ride staring out of the window, feeling restless and slightly silly. By the third day, though, something changed. Instead of fighting the feeling, I let my thoughts drift, and I became curious about the small things I had walked past for years, like the old man who feeds pigeons outside the station every evening. At home, I dug out a sketchbook I had given up on in junior high and filled ten pages with drawings of the people I had noticed. I wouldn’t say the week turned me into a new person, and I was honestly glad to get my phone back at the end. Still, I now keep it in my bag during the ride home, just to find out where my mind will wander.

translation_zh.text:
我們大多數人都努力不讓自己感到無聊，而在人手一機的時代，要逃離這種感覺再容易不過了。但無聊真的是需要逃避的東西嗎？在下面兩篇文章中，一位科學作家說明研究人員對無聊有哪些了解，一位高中生則描述她給無聊一次機會之後發生了什麼事。

A　無聊有什麼用
無聊常被說成只是「沒事可做」，但心理學家的定義更精確：它是想投入一件令人滿足的活動、卻找不到這樣的活動時那種不愉快的感覺。這樣看來，無聊並不是懶惰的表現。它比較像一個警報，告訴我們正在做的事已經無法滿足我們的需要，是時候換做別的事了。無聊也可能有一個隱藏的好處。當大腦沒有東西可抓住時，往往會開始神遊，而在這些做白日夢的時刻，人常會在不同的想法之間產生意想不到的連結。在一個知名的實驗中，先花一段時間做非常枯燥工作的人，之後想出的點子比跳過這項工作的人更有創意。現在的問題是，我們很少讓無聊持續夠久、好讓它對我們有所幫助。一覺得坐立不安，我們就伸手拿螢幕；研究人員懷疑，這種速成的解方長遠來看反而可能讓我們更無聊。

B　沒有手機的一週
上個月，我們的英文老師要全班放學後一週不用手機。頭兩天，我簡直坐立難安。每次坐上公車，我的手就一直伸向空空的口袋，整趟車程都盯著窗外，覺得焦躁又有點傻。不過到了第三天，有些事改變了。我不再抗拒這種感覺，而是讓思緒漂流，開始對那些我經過多年的小事物感到好奇，例如每天傍晚在車站外餵鴿子的老先生。回到家，我翻出國中時就放棄的素描本，用十頁畫下我注意到的人。我不會說這一週讓我脫胎換骨，而且老實說，最後拿回手機時我很高興。不過，現在搭車回家時，我會把手機放在包包裡，只是想知道我的思緒會飄到哪裡去。
